newsitem.title: USA: New baseball tells you how fast you throw it.
newsitem.headline: New baseball tells you how fast you throw it.

text.p: It's an argument kids have been having for as long as there has been sandlot baseball -- "My fastball's faster than yours."

Rawlings Sporting Goods Co. Inc.'s new Radar Ball may help prove whose fastball is faster, at a price of about $35. While this is three to four times the cost of a standard Major League baseball, it's a lot less expensive than buying a radar gun, typically used to measure fastballs -- and speeding cars.
The Radar Ball has nothing to do with radar.
Developed by Canadian Dave Zakutin, 25, as a college engineering project, the Radar Ball contains a microprocessor that is activated by tapping the ball.

The processor, calibrated to a set distance -- such as the 60-feet, 6-inches between a major league pitcher's mound and home plate -- measures how long it takes the ball to travel from the pitcher's hand to the catcher's mitt and then converts this to miles per hour.
"It actually tested out within one mile an hour each time of what the radar gun was telling us," Randy Black, vice president of marketing for St. Louis-based Rawlings, said.
Zakutin initially tried to create a speed-sensing ball seven years ago after seeing a model by another company.
"I thought I could probably build something like that and build it better," Zakutin said, adding that he thought "he could make my money in a few weeks and take the rest of the summer off."
But developing the ball was harder than he thought and Rawlings was not interested in the first product.
Two years ago, he returned to the baseball as a fourth-year engineering project at the University of Waterloo in Ontario.
"We just take a regular baseball now and poke a little hole in it and put in a self-contained" computer, Zakutin said.

He and two players from a local baseball camp went to Rawlings headquarters in St. Louis in 1996 to make a presentation to Rawlings' top marketing people, who initially did not seem receptive, Zakutin said.
"They were really sceptical that these three kids would have anything they'd be interested in," Zakutin said. But the executives were sold when they went outside and played with the ball, he said.
Unlike previous models that had a hard plastic shell, the Radar Ball is a typical baseball that just happens to have a computer inside.
"This looks like, feels like, tastes like, throws like a regular baseball," Black said.
The one thing you can't do with it is hit it with a bat. That cancels the one-year warranty.

The Radar Ball is one step in Rawlings' attempt to branch out from its traditional baseball and glove offerings. The company is also trying to crack into the $100 million-plus market for aluminum baseball and softball bats with what it calls a Power Forged bat. The new bat has a larger "Sweet Spot" that makes it easier for batters to make solid contact with a ball.
"Kids need and want to have a little more fast-moving sport," Black said of Rawlings' attempt to offer more innovative products. "They're looking for more perfomance oriented equipment."
Rawlings, which is the official baseball supplier to the Major Leagues, was hurt by the 1994 baseball strike and decline in the sport's popularity.

For the nine months ended May 31, Rawlings earned $6.2 million, or 80 cents a share, on sales of $121.0 million. A year earlier it earned $6.1 million, or 79 cents a share, on sales of $126.0 million.
Rawlings will begin shipping the bats to retailers in the fall. But the Radar Ball won't be available until early next year.
Rawlings will not say how many Radar Balls it expects to sell. The ball will be both marketed to baseball teams to use for training and for children and parents to use in the backyard.
Peter Schaeffer, an analyst who follows the company for Dillon, Read estimated the company could sell 500,000 Radar Balls for Christmas 1998.
Zakutin, meanwhile, has a royalty agreement with Rawlings and is operating his own business in Canada, trying to devleop other products.
